title: Three Rising Values in Order
statement:
Given an integer array nums, return true if you can pick three positions i < j < k with nums[i] < nums[j] < nums[k]. The three values do not have to be next to each other, but they must keep their order in the array and rise strictly.

Otherwise return false. Aim for one pass with O(1) extra memory.

examples.why: 5, 6, 7. The 1 that comes later does not undo the fact that 5 came before 6.
Equal values do not count as rising, so the best you get is 2, 3.

hints: For a middle value, all you need to know is whether something smaller came before it and something bigger comes after it.
Scan left to right and remember the smallest value so far, and the smallest value that already has something smaller before it.
Keep first and second. For each x: if x ≤ first, first = x; else if x ≤ second, second = x; else you found a third value bigger than both, return true.

explain.intuition:
Track two numbers while scanning: first, the smallest value seen, and second, the smallest value seen that has a smaller value somewhere before it. If any later value is bigger than second, the triple exists.

The part that feels wrong: when a new small value replaces first, it now sits after second in the array. That is fine. second still stands for a pair that really happened (the old first came before it). Lowering first only makes it easier to start a new better pair later. Keeping both values as small as possible never throws away a chance.
steps: For each x: if x ≤ first, set first = x.
Else if x ≤ second, set second = x (now some smaller value comes before it).
pitfalls: Using < instead of ≤ in the updates. Then equal values slip through to the third branch and [2, 2, 2] wrongly returns true.
Thinking you must reset second when first drops. Example 1 needs the old second = 6 to survive the 1.
Checking only adjacent elements. The three values may be far apart.

solutions.title: Try every triple
solutions.idea: Three nested loops over i < j < k.

solutions.title: Prefix minimum and suffix maximum
solutions.idea: A position works as the middle if the smallest value before it is lower and the largest value after it is higher. Precompute both.

solutions.title: Two running thresholds
solutions.idea: Keep the smallest value and the smallest value that has something smaller before it. Anything above both completes a triple.

followups: Return the three indexes, not just true or false. What extra value do you need to remember?
Generalise to a rising run of length k. How does this connect to the longest increasing subsequence?
